text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- More than half of 13-year-old in the Taby area drink alcohol regularly with most getting spirits from their parents, a new study has shown. Culture and Leisure head Lennart Bjork said the figures are frightening.
A second study finds that smuggling of spirits into Sweden cost the state 1.5 billion crowns in lost tax income last year.

- Swedish exports are slipping to Europe but have risen 13 percent to Africa, America and Asia, according to figures from Statistics Sweden for the first 10 months of 1996. In total exports amounted to 467.7 billion crowns in that period compared to 471 billion crowns a year earlier.

- Misuse of the designer drug ecstasy is increasing among Swedish teenagers. Last year 108 teenagers under the influence of ecstasy were taken to the Maria clinic for treatment of youngsters on drugs or alcohol. This was double as many as in 1995. Preliminary figures estimate 1,258 teenagers had contact with ecstasy last year.

- Sweden is still the tops in the small world of the sport bandy, beating Russia in the rand finals on Sunday 10-5 (6-1) before a crowd of 10,217. This was Sweden's seventh Grand Masters gold in bandy and the third consecutive win.

- Stefan Persson, head of Swedish fashion retailer Hennes & Mauritz, speaks out in an interview with the paper against tax proposals. He says paying 100 percent tax is not right. Persson says he is happy with the success of his company and wants to expand further in Germany among other countries. Persson and his relatives hold 46.5 percent of capital and 74 percent of votes of H&M.

- It will be impossible to close one of the two nuclear reactors at Barseback on Sweden's southwest coast in 1998, according to trade union energy expert Claes Hellgren. He is very critical of the agreement between the ruling Social Democrats and Centre and Left parties designed to phase out nuclear power in Sweden.

- Telecommunication stocks will be in focus this week with both Ericsson and Nokia due to release their earnings reports for 1996. Stock prices have already been driven up amid high expectations. Ericsson is to report its results on Tuesday and Nokia on Thursday.

- Sweden's housing loan market will be changed when the European Union's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) begins in early 1999. Whether Sweden chooses to join EMU from the start or not, it will increase competition in the market, industry groups say. Overseas financial groups will start offering services to the private sector and not just the public sector and big companies as is currently the case.
